ToolHeader.title: Open Graph Generator
ToolHeader.description: See how your link will look when it is shared on Telegram or X, and take the og: and twitter: tags away ready to paste. Nothing you type is sent anywhere; the image is opened in your own browser, only to measure it.

import.title: Bring in existing tags
import.hint: Paste your page's head section, or just the meta tags, and the form fills itself from them. No request is made — it is all parsed in your browser.
import.nothing: No meta tags this tool recognises were found in that text.

rescrape.hint: Updated your tags but still seeing the old card? Refresh the platform's cache here:

form.title: Title
form.descriptionPlaceholder: A sentence or two about what the page is
form.imageHint: Must be an absolute URL starting with https://. A relative path (/og.png) will not work.

preview.title: Share card
preview.truncation: {platform} shows roughly {title} characters of the title and {description} of the description — the rest is cut.

issues.title: Checks
issues.clean: All good — the card will render in full.
issues.titleMissing: No title. Without one, platforms pick the first text they find on the page, and it is rarely the text you wanted.
issues.titleLong: The title is {length} characters. Most places cut it after {max}.
issues.titleTooLong: The title is {length} characters — longer than {max}. Every platform will cut it.
issues.descriptionMissing: No description. The line under the title in the card will be empty.
issues.descriptionLong: The description is {length} characters. Search results cut it after {max}.
issues.descriptionTooLong: The description is {length} characters — longer than {max}. Half of it will not be shown.
issues.imageMissing: No image. A card without one renders at half the size and gets far fewer clicks.
issues.imageRelative: The image URL is relative. Crawlers resolve it against their own host and find nothing — use a full https:// address.
issues.imageUnreachable: The image could not be loaded. The URL may be wrong, or the host may be blocking requests from other sites.
issues.imageTooSmall: The image is {width} × {height} — too small. Platforms drop images with an edge below {min} pixels entirely.
issues.imageRatio: The image ratio is {ratio}:1 ({width} × {height}). Cards are built for 1.91:1, so part of it will be cropped away.
issues.imageAltMissing: No image description (alt). A screen-reader user is told nothing about what the picture shows.
issues.urlMissing: No page URL. og:url is the link the card points at and doubles as the canonical address.
issues.urlRelative: The page URL is not absolute — it has to start with https://.
issues.largeCardNoImage: The card type is “large image” but there is no image. X falls back to the small card, and your choice does nothing.

reference.title: What each platform shows
reference.intro: Open Graph is how you decide what your page looks like when it is shared. Without the tags, the platform picks some text and some image off the page itself. The numbers below are the approximate points where text gets cut — not hard rules, but worth writing your title against.

telegram.name: Telegram
telegram.note: Reads og: tags, not twitter:. The one that matters most for an Uzbek audience.

x.name: X (Twitter)
x.note: Falls back to og: when twitter: is absent. summary_large_image needs an image.

facebook.name: Facebook
facebook.note: Reads og: tags only. The cache can be refreshed through the Sharing Debugger.

linkedin.name: LinkedIn
linkedin.note: Reads og: tags and caches them for a long time — refresh via Post Inspector.

image.title: Image size
image.body: {width} × {height} — every large card is built around that 1.91:1 ratio. An image with an edge below {min} pixels is not shown at all. And the URL must be absolute: a relative path is the single commonest reason a share card has no picture.

cache.title: Why your change is not showing
cache.body: Platforms cache the tags they read the first time — Facebook and LinkedIn for a long while. If the old card keeps appearing after you have fixed the tags, that is usually not a bug: re-scrape the URL in the Facebook Sharing Debugger or the LinkedIn Post Inspector.

whatIsOg.question: What is Open Graph, and do I need it?
whatIsOg.answer: Open Graph is the set of meta tags that decide which title, description and image appear when your page is shared on social media. Without them the platform picks its own text and image off the page, which is how a card ends up showing your navigation menu or a random picture. If your links get shared on Telegram or anywhere social, you need them.

notUpdating.question: I updated the tags but the card is still the old one. Why?
notUpdating.answer: Almost always caching. Platforms store what they read the first time they fetch your page — Facebook and LinkedIn keep it for a long while, and Telegram caches on its own servers. The fix is to re-scrape the URL in the Facebook Sharing Debugger or the LinkedIn Post Inspector. For Telegram, testing with a changed query string such as ?v=2 is the usual workaround.

imageSize.question: What image should og:image point at?
imageSize.answer: 1200 × 630 pixels, a 1.91:1 ratio — every large card is designed around it. Platforms drop images with an edge below 200 pixels entirely. Most important of all: the URL must be absolute. A relative path like /og.png does not work, because the crawler resolves it against its own domain, and that is the number-one reason a card has no picture. This tool loads your image in your browser and measures the real dimensions.

twitterNeeded.question: If I have og: tags, do I also need twitter: tags?
twitterNeeded.answer: Mostly no. X falls back to the og: tags for the title, description and image, so repeating them only creates a second copy to keep in sync. The two that genuinely do something are twitter:card, which decides whether the card is large or small, and twitter:site, which attributes it to your account — which is exactly what this tool writes.

nextjs.question: Where do these tags go in a Next.js project?
nextjs.answer: In the App Router you do not write meta tags by hand — you export a metadata object from page.tsx or layout.tsx and Next renders the tags for you. Pick the “Next.js” shape and the output is that object, ready to paste into the file. For the Pages Router or a plain HTML site, take the “HTML” shape and put it in the page's head section.
